mappings.note: Two clearly separated asks: p, n and e from A = 24 and Z = 12 (LO-4), then 'illustrate the arrangement' as 2,8,2 over K, L, M (LO-2). The biology framing is decoration - nothing about muscle contraction is graded, so no CG5.

Three genuinely separate strands, which is why this is a three-code item: name the element from its shell diagram (LO-5, interpret data to classify), give valence electrons and valency (LO-3), and supply the symbol Li / N / Al / F (C-1.3-LO-2, 'recognise and accurately apply the chemical [symbols]' - the object word is missing from the row but is recoverable from LO-28's orphaned 'for the first eighteen elements according to IUPAC'). This is the one item in the chapter that asks for a symbol rather than a name.

PARTIAL FIT. The answer is the stationary-orbit postulate: an accelerating charge would radiate and spiral in, so orbits of fixed energy are needed. LO-2 is the only outcome naming energy levels and C1.1 the only intact row naming Bohr's model; no outcome states atomic stability or radiation. No CG7 - the graded content is the mechanism, not the fact that one model replaced another.

Twin of P13 and mapped the same way: the mass number arrives as a superscript that must be read as a convention (LO-6) before n = 70 - 31 can be taken (LO-4). N12 states its numbers in words and gets LO-4 alone - that is the split inside the numerical family.
Plain LO-4 in both limbs: n = A - Z and e = p for a neutral atom, both numbers handed over in words. No notation to decode (so no LO-6) and no element named (so no LO-5).

The five rows are LO-4 arithmetic run from whichever two cells are given, but the last column asks for the NAME of each element, which is LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify elements accurately'. Not C-1.3-LO-2: names are wanted, not symbols - the reverse of N9.

Seven parts, four strands, and the three-code cap bites here. LO-4 carries (i), (ii) and (vi); LO-3 carries (v) valence electrons and (vii) the isotope relation; LO-2 carries (iv) the 2,8,7 configuration. The fourth strand, (iii) identify chlorine, would be LO-5 and is the one I dropped, being one ask of seven.

Nothing is calculated - each of the four parts asks which DEFINITION the quantity depends on (Z on protons only, mass number on nucleons only, atomic mass on everything present, charge on the p-e balance). That is LO-3's 'explain ... atomic number, atomic mass' plus LO-1 for which particle carries the charge and which the mass. Deliberately not LO-4, which is for producing counts.

POOR FIT, recorded rather than forced. Acharya Kanada's parmanu belongs to Indian philosophical literature, i.e. knowledge from another curricular area - CG5. C5.1 ('how literature and arts have influenced Science') is the nearest competency but names literature and arts, not philosophy, and neither of its two outcomes (LO-28, LO-43) is about anything but drawing diagrams. No learning outcome covers the pre-scientific history of the atom.

Textbook LO-1: three particles identified purely from relative charge (-1, +1, 0) and relative mass. The cleanest instance of 'differentiate between subatomic particles based on their charge' in the chapter.

The distractors are all model statements and the one correct reading of a sharp deflection is a dense positive centre - LO-1's position clause. Option (C) makes energy levels the trap, so LO-2 is what this item tests AGAINST, not what it tests.

PARTIAL FIT, same gap as P3. What is graded is the cathode-ray observation itself (rays run cathode to anode), and curriculum 82 has no outcome for discovery experiments. LO-1 is the nearest because the observation is what establishes the electron as the negative subatomic particle.

The 2n-squared capacities of M and N are literally LO-5's 'maximum number of electrons in a shell' read off a table, and LO-2 supplies the K, L, M, N scheme the table is built on. Unlike P15 this asks for shell CAPACITY, not for a particular element's configuration - that is the split between the two shell items.

Statement 3 is the discriminator and it is false because alpha particles are REPELLED by a like charge; statements 1 and 2 are about empty space and a dense centre. All three are charge-and-position claims, i.e. LO-1.

The trajectories have to be read back to a uniform positive sphere (P) against a concentrated nucleus (Q) - LO-1's position clause. LO-28 comes close - its surviving clause names labelled diagrams of Thomson's and Rutherford's models - but the student READS a supplied diagram rather than drawing one, and the row is a shredded fusion whose verb is missing (see report), so I keep LO-28 to the one item that asks for the drawing, S57.

The fact wanted is the electron's negative charge (LO-1), but the distractor is -1.602, so the item really tests the conventional RELATIVE charge scale rather than the coulomb value - LO-6's scientific conventions. That trap is what separates this from O2, which needs no convention.

Same proton count, different neutron count, so W and X - the isotope definition from LO-3, applied by reading a four-row table, which is LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify'. Not LO-4: the table hands over p and n directly and no mass number need be produced.

The watermelon analogy is scored on which part maps to the continuous positive charge and which to the embedded electrons - LO-1's position clause, the same as P2. A family that honestly shares one outcome: both are Thomson-analogy items and I found no legal code that separates them.

POOR FIT. Absorption of energy to jump to a higher stationary state is not stated by any outcome in curriculum 82. LO-2 is cited because the answer depends on the shells being discrete levels with a fixed order (K below M), and C1.1 because it is the only intact row that names Bohr's model.

Ten electrons have to be laid out as 2,8 (LO-2) and then the table read to pick the unreactive one (LO-5, 'interpret data ... to classify elements accurately'). LO-3 was considered for the octet idea, but the item never asks for valence electrons or valency as such - it asks which element the data mark out.

POOR FIT, and the MCQ twin of N5 - mapped identically on purpose. The four clues are model descriptions to be put in historical order, which no learning outcome states; CG7's 'Science is ever evolving' is the only matching text and C1.1 the one intact row naming Bohr's model.

Counting p and n off the diagram gives Z = 6 and A = 14 (LO-4); the third ask, valency 4 from a 2,4 configuration, is LO-3's 'valence electrons, valency'. Not LO-5: no element is classified or named, the answer stops at the three quantities.

POOR FIT. What an alpha particle IS - a helium nucleus - is nowhere in curriculum 82; the alpha particle is not one of LO-1's three subatomic particles. LO-1 is the nearest because the correct option is phrased entirely as a count of protons and neutrons, which is the only part of the answer any outcome touches.

Isobars from LO-3, picked out of a Z-and-A table, which is LO-5's interpretation clause. Mapped the same as O9 because the two items are the same task on the other relation - the honest distinction is isotopes vs isobars, and LO-3 names both, so no code separates them.

PARTIAL FIT. What is graded is the shape of an investigation - setup, observation, conclusion, model - and curriculum 82 has no outcome about scientific method. The material being ordered is the nucleus finding, so LO-1. No CG7: unlike N5 and O13 this orders one experiment's steps, not a century of models.
